specStatements.text: When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. These liquids and solutions are able to conduct electricity and are called electrolytes.

Passing an electric current through electrolytes causes the ions to move to the electrodes. Positively charged ions move to the negative electrode (the cathode), and negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode (the anode). Ions are discharged at the electrodes producing elements. This process is called electrolysis.

(HT only) Throughout Section 4.4.3 Higher Tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes during electrolysis, and may be required to complete and balance supplied half equations.

When a simple ionic compound (eg lead bromide) is electrolysed in the molten state using inert electrodes, the metal (lead) is produced at the cathode and the non-metal (bromine) is produced at the anode.
Students should be able to predict the products of the electrolysis of binary ionic compounds in the molten state.

Metals can be extracted from molten compounds using electrolysis. Electrolysis is used if the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon or if the metal reacts with carbon. Large amounts of energy are used in the extraction process to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current.
Aluminium is manufactured by the electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite using carbon as the positive electrode (anode).
explain why a mixture is used as the electrolyte
explain why the positive electrode must be continually replaced.
The ions discharged when an aqueous solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.
At the negative electrode (cathode), hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
At the positive electrode (anode), oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions when the halogen is produced.
This happens because in the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions that are discharged.
Required practical 3: investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes. This should be an investigation involving developing a hypothesis.
During electrolysis, at the cathode (negative electrode), positively charged ions gain electrons and so the reactions are reductions.
At the anode (positive electrode), negatively charged ions lose electrons and so the reactions are oxidations.
Reactions at electrodes can be represented by half equations, for example:
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
and
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂ O + 4e⁻
or
4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂ O

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Throughout Section 4.4.3 Higher Tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes during electrolysis, and may be required to complete and balance supplied half equations.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Half equations are treated as Higher Tier only. Every concept, misconception and question that asks a student to write, complete, balance or interpret a half equation (c17 to c21, m25 to m31, q22 to q30) carries tier "higher". Foundation-tier items ask only which element appears at which electrode, never for an equation with electrons in it.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to predict the products of the electrolysis of binary ionic compounds in the molten state.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Molten-state prediction questions (q07, q08) use only binary compounds - one metal and one non-metal, such as magnesium chloride and aluminium oxide. No molten compound containing a polyatomic ion is set for prediction, and the aqueous rules of 4.4.3.4 are never applied to a molten compound.

scopeNotes.statement: When a simple ionic compound (eg lead bromide) is electrolysed in the molten state using inert electrodes ...
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every cell described here uses inert electrodes such as graphite or platinum (concept c05), except the carbon anode of the aluminium cell, which the specification names explicitly. Electrolysis with reactive electrodes - electroplating and the purification of copper - is not taught, because 4.4.3 does not include it.

scopeNotes.statement: Aluminium is manufactured by the electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite using carbon as the positive electrode (anode).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The aluminium content is kept to what the specification states: the molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, carbon as the positive electrode, why a mixture is used and why that electrode is replaced. No cell voltages, currents, yields, costs in figures or plant details are introduced.

concepts.definition: An ionic compound that has been melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Electrolytes conduct electricity.
The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte makes the ions move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to produce elements.
The negative electrode. Positively charged ions move to it.
The positive electrode. Negatively charged ions move to it.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not take part in the reactions of the cell, so the products come only from the electrolyte.
The loss of charge by an ion at an electrode, as electrons are gained or lost, turning the ion into a neutral atom or molecule of an element.
An ionic compound made of just two elements, one metal and one non-metal, such as lead bromide or magnesium chloride.

concepts.term: Products of a molten binary compound
concepts.definition: When a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Obtaining a metal from its molten compound by electrolysis. It is used when the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or when the metal reacts with carbon.
Large amounts of energy are used in extraction by electrolysis, both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.
The compound mixed with aluminium oxide in the aluminium cell. The mixture melts at a lower temperature than aluminium oxide alone, so less energy is needed.
The positive electrode is made of carbon. Oxygen produced there reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is worn away and must be replaced continually.
At the negative electrode hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; otherwise the metal is produced.
At the positive electrode oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.
In an aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and these ions can be discharged at the electrodes.
A testable idea, put forward before the experiment, that predicts what will happen and can be supported or disproved by the results of Required practical 3.
Gain of electrons. At the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions there are reductions.
Loss of electrons. At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions there are oxidations.
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode only, including the electrons gained or lost, balanced for both atoms and charge.
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, which may also be written as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop with hydrogen. A glowing splint relights in oxygen, and damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine.

misconceptions.question: Does solid lead bromide conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. It conducts only once it has been melted or dissolved.
misconceptions.misconception: Ionic solids conduct because they are made of charged ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that ionic compounds contain charged particles and assume charge alone is enough, without asking whether the charges can move.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction needs charges that are free to move. In the solid the ions are locked in fixed positions in the lattice; melting or dissolving frees them, which is why only the melt and the solution are electrolytes.

misconceptions.question: Are there ions in solid sodium chloride?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The solid is already made of ions, held in a lattice.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting or dissolving is what turns neutral atoms into ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ions are first met in the context of a reaction that forms them, so any change that makes conduction possible is read as the moment the ions are made.
misconceptions.correction: The ions exist in the solid compound already. Melting or dissolving does not create them; it only lets them move.

misconceptions.question: What carries the current through molten lead bromide?
misconceptions.correct: Moving ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons flow through the liquid, as they do through a wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The circuit outside the cell does carry electrons, and students extend that single picture to the liquid inside the cell.
misconceptions.correction: In the external circuit electrons flow; in the electrolyte the current is carried by ions moving to the electrodes, where electrons are transferred.

misconceptions.question: Which electrode is the cathode?
misconceptions.correct: The negative one.
misconceptions.misconception: The cathode is positive and the anode is negative.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two unfamiliar words are learned as a pair without an anchor, so the labels are attached to the wrong signs.
misconceptions.correction: Cathode means the negative electrode, which attracts positive ions; anode means the positive electrode, which attracts negative ions.

misconceptions.question: Where do positive ions go?
misconceptions.correct: To the negative electrode, the cathode.
misconceptions.misconception: Positive ions travel to the positive electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under pressure students match the words 'positive ion' to 'positive electrode' rather than applying the rule that opposite charges attract.
misconceptions.correction: Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions move to the positive electrode.

misconceptions.question: What is made when ions are discharged?
misconceptions.correct: Elements.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrolysis makes new compounds at the electrodes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most reactions students meet make compounds, so they expect a product more complicated than a single element.
misconceptions.correction: Discharge removes the charge from an ion, leaving neutral atoms that join to form an element: a metal or a non-metal, never a new compound.

misconceptions.question: Which electrode gives the metal in a molten compound?
misconceptions.correct: The cathode, the negative electrode.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal appears at the anode and the non-metal at the cathode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metals are strongly associated with positive things, so the metal is placed at the positive electrode without tracking the charge on its ion.
misconceptions.correction: The metal forms a positive ion, so it is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode); the non-metal ion is negative and goes to the anode.

misconceptions.question: Can hydrogen be produced from a molten compound?
misconceptions.correct: Not from a dry molten compound, because there is no water in it.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen and oxygen are produced whatever is electrolysed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The aqueous rules are learned as facts about electrolysis in general, and are then applied to a molten compound where no water is present.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen and hydroxide ions come from water. A molten compound contains no water, so the products can only be the two elements in the compound.

misconceptions.question: Is Br⁻ the product at the anode?
misconceptions.correct: No. Bromine, Br₂, is the product.
misconceptions.misconception: The ion itself is given off at the electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students name the particle they know is attracted to the electrode and stop there, missing the electron transfer that discharges it.
misconceptions.correction: At the electrode the ion is discharged: bromide ions lose electrons and form bromine molecules, an element with no charge.

misconceptions.question: Why is electrolysis used for aluminium?
misconceptions.correct: Because aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrolysis is chosen because it is the cheaper method.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume industry always picks the cheapest route, so the method actually used must be the cheap one.
misconceptions.correction: Electrolysis is expensive, using large amounts of energy to melt the compound and produce the current. It is used only when carbon cannot do the job.

misconceptions.question: Could carbon extract aluminium if the furnace were hotter?
misconceptions.correct: No. Reactivity, not temperature, is what decides.
misconceptions.misconception: Any metal can be extracted with carbon if it is heated enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heat is seen as a way of forcing any reaction to happen, so the reactivity order is treated as something temperature can overcome.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon can only remove oxygen from the oxide of a metal less reactive than carbon. Aluminium is more reactive, so it must be extracted by electrolysis.

misconceptions.question: Is aluminium oxide dissolved in water for electrolysis?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is melted, mixed with cryolite.
misconceptions.misconception: The aluminium cell uses a solution of aluminium oxide in water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most electrolysis the student has seen in class uses solutions, so a solution is assumed here too.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium oxide is insoluble, and water would give hydrogen at the cathode instead of aluminium. The electrolyte is a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite.

misconceptions.question: What does the cryolite do?
misconceptions.correct: It lowers the melting point of the mixture, so less energy is needed.
misconceptions.misconception: Cryolite is a catalyst that speeds the electrolysis up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Something added that makes the process work better' is filed under catalyst, the only such idea many students have.
misconceptions.correction: Cryolite is not a catalyst. Aluminium oxide melts at over 2000 °C; the mixture with cryolite melts at a much lower temperature, saving energy.

misconceptions.question: Where does the aluminium come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the aluminium oxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Cryolite supplies the aluminium ions that are discharged.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cryolite is named in the same sentence as the aluminium and is assumed to be the source of the metal.
misconceptions.correction: The aluminium comes from the aluminium oxide. The cryolite is there to lower the melting point of the mixture.

misconceptions.question: Why is the carbon anode replaced?
misconceptions.correct: Oxygen made there reacts with the hot carbon and wears it away.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon electrode simply melts in the heat of the cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Wearing away is explained by the most obvious feature of the cell, its high temperature, rather than by a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon does not melt at the temperature of the cell. Oxygen is discharged at the anode and reacts with the hot carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the electrode is eaten away.

misconceptions.question: Does the anode dissolve in the electrolyte?
misconceptions.correct: No. It reacts with the oxygen produced on it.
misconceptions.misconception: The positive electrode dissolves away because it is positive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electroplating and copper purification, where a metal anode really does dissolve, are half-remembered and applied to an inert carbon anode.
misconceptions.correction: An inert electrode does not dissolve. The carbon anode is lost because oxygen discharged on it burns it away as carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Is the metal always produced at the cathode in a solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal in the dissolved compound is always made at the cathode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The molten-state rule 'metal at the cathode' is carried over to solutions, where water also supplies ions.
misconceptions.correction: In solution the cathode product depends on relative reactivity: a metal less reactive than hydrogen is produced, but if the metal is more reactive, hydrogen is produced instead.

misconceptions.question: When is hydrogen made at the cathode?
misconceptions.correct: When the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is made when the metal is less reactive than hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is memorised as a pair of words without a reason, so the comparison is easily reversed under exam pressure.
misconceptions.correction: The less reactive element is the one discharged. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen it stays in solution and hydrogen is produced.

misconceptions.question: Is oxygen always the anode product in solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. A halide solution gives the halogen instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is produced at the anode whatever the solution contains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'water gives oxygen' half of the rule is remembered and the halide exception is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, in which case the halogen - chlorine, bromine or iodine - is produced.

misconceptions.question: Does sodium sulfate solution give sulfur at an electrode?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sulfate is not a halide, so oxygen is produced.
misconceptions.misconception: The non-metal part of the dissolved compound is always discharged.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students split the compound name in two and expect both halves to appear, without checking whether the ion is a halide.
misconceptions.correction: Only halide ions are discharged in place of hydroxide. With sulfate, nitrate or a similar ion, oxygen is produced at the anode from hydroxide ions.

misconceptions.question: Where do hydrogen ions in a solution come from?
misconceptions.correct: From water molecules breaking down.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen ions come from the dissolved compound splitting up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track only the compound they added and forget that water itself supplies ions.
misconceptions.correction: In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions; these are the extra ions available for discharge.

misconceptions.question: Does water break down into hydrogen and oxygen molecules in the solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. It produces hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Water in the solution splits straight into H₂ and O₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The overall result of electrolysing dilute acid is remembered as 'water splits into hydrogen and oxygen', and that summary replaces the ion step.
misconceptions.correction: Water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. The gases appear only after those ions are discharged at the electrodes.

misconceptions.question: Why are graphite electrodes used in Required practical 3?
misconceptions.correct: Because they conduct and take no part in the reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: Any material that conducts will do as an electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The electrode is thought of only as a way of getting current into the liquid, not as a possible reactant.
misconceptions.correction: The electrode must be inert as well as conducting. A reactive electrode would take part in the reaction and change the products being investigated.

misconceptions.question: What does a squeaky pop with a lit splint show?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas tests are muddled, so a squeaky pop with a lit splint is credited to a gas other than hydrogen, such as oxygen or chlorine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two gas tests are learned together and the splint is the memorable part, so which splint goes with which gas gets swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.

misconceptions.question: Is gaining electrons oxidation or reduction?
misconceptions.correct: Reduction.
misconceptions.misconception: Gaining electrons is oxidation and losing them is reduction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word reduction suggests something being made smaller, which fits losing a particle better than gaining one.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons. At the cathode positive ions gain electrons, so cathode reactions are reductions.

misconceptions.question: Does the sign of the electrode tell you whether it is oxidation?
misconceptions.correct: No. What matters is whether electrons are lost or gained by the ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The positive electrode must be where reduction happens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Positive' is matched with 'gain' and 'negative' with 'loss', so the sign of the electrode is used instead of the electron transfer.
misconceptions.correction: At the anode (positive) negative ions lose electrons, so it is oxidation. At the cathode (negative) positive ions gain electrons, so it is reduction.

misconceptions.question: Which side of a half equation do the electrons go on?
misconceptions.correct: On the left for a reduction, on the right for an oxidation.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons are put on the wrong side of the arrow because the side is not linked to gain or loss: they belong with the reactants at the cathode (the ion gains them) and with the products at the anode (the ion loses them).
misconceptions.whyItArises: The half equation is copied as a pattern rather than read as electrons being supplied to, or taken from, the ion.
misconceptions.correction: At the cathode electrons are gained, so they appear with the reactants: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. At the anode they are lost, so they appear with the products.

misconceptions.question: Does a half equation have to balance for charge as well as atoms?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, for both.
misconceptions.misconception: A half equation is treated as balanced when just one requirement is met, the atoms alone or the total charge alone, instead of requiring both atoms and charge to balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is taught first with ordinary equations, where only atoms are counted, so the charges are not checked.
misconceptions.correction: The number of electrons must make the total charge the same on each side, as well as the atoms balancing. H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ balances for charge (zero on each side) but not for atoms, so it is still wrong; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ passes both tests.

misconceptions.question: What does – 4e⁻ on the left of an equation mean?
misconceptions.correct: That four electrons are removed, that is, lost.
misconceptions.misconception: A minus sign in front of electrons means they are added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the equation as arithmetic on one line and take any term on the left as a reactant being supplied.
misconceptions.correction: 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ say the same thing: the hydroxide ions lose four electrons.

misconceptions.question: How many electrons does Al³⁺ need to become Al?
misconceptions.correct: Three.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of electrons is taken from the formula rather than the charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a number in the formula to copy, and use a subscript or the number of ions instead of the size of the charge.
misconceptions.correction: The charge on the ion sets the number of electrons: Al³⁺ carries three positive charges, so Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.

misconceptions.question: Is discharging an ion the same as neutralisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a transfer of electrons, described as oxidation or reduction.
misconceptions.misconception: An ion losing its charge at an electrode is neutralisation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutralisation is the only process students have met in which charge disappears, so the word is reused for discharge.
misconceptions.correction: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. At an electrode the ion gains or loses electrons: gain of electrons is reduction, loss of electrons is oxidation.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy go in extraction by electrolysis?
misconceptions.correct: Into melting the compound and producing the electrical current.
misconceptions.misconception: The cost of the process lies in mining and purifying the ore.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know extraction is expensive and attach the cost to the stage they can picture most easily.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific: large amounts of energy are used to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current.

misconceptions.question: Does the ion with the biggest charge get discharged first?
misconceptions.correct: No. Relative reactivity decides.
misconceptions.misconception: The size of the charge on an ion decides whether it is discharged.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is the property students use to work out which electrode an ion moves to, so it is reused for the next decision as well.
misconceptions.correction: Charge decides which electrode an ion travels to. Which of the ions arriving there is actually discharged depends on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.

misconceptions.question: Is 'the solution turned blue' a hypothesis?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is an observation.
misconceptions.misconception: A hypothesis is a description of what was seen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hypothesis, observation and conclusion are all written in the same practical account, so the words blur together.
misconceptions.correction: A hypothesis is a testable idea put forward before the experiment, predicting what will happen and why. An observation is what is recorded during it.

misconceptions.question: Is 'which gas forms at the cathode?' a hypothesis?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is a question the investigation asks.
misconceptions.misconception: A hypothesis is the question you are trying to answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Investigations start from a question, so the question is taken to be the hypothesis itself.
misconceptions.correction: The question sets the aim; the hypothesis is the answer you propose in advance, stated so that results can support or disprove it.

mcqs.stem: Solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten lead bromide does. Why?

options.text: Melting changes the neutral atoms into charged ions
options.rationale: Melting is confused with the electron transfer that formed the compound, so the ions seem to be made at this moment.

options.text: Melting releases electrons that then carry the charge
options.rationale: The picture of electrons flowing in a wire is transferred to the liquid instead of using moving ions.

options.text: Melting frees the ions so they can move through the liquid
options.rationale: Conduction needs charges free to move; melting breaks up the lattice and the ions move about within the liquid.

options.text: Solid lead bromide contains no charged particles
options.rationale: A student who thinks charge alone causes conduction has to explain the solid by denying it contains charges.

mcqs.stem: Which of these can act as an electrolyte?

options.text: Sodium chloride dissolved in pure water
options.rationale: Dissolving separates the ions and lets them move about in the solution, so the solution conducts.

options.text: Sodium chloride kept as a dry white solid
options.rationale: The solid contains ions but they are fixed in the lattice, so it is not an electrolyte.

options.text: A copper wire carrying an electric current
options.rationale: A metal conducts by moving electrons, not ions, so it is a conductor but not an electrolyte.

options.text: Sugar dissolved in some warm water
options.rationale: Sugar is not ionic; the solution contains molecules only, so nothing charged can move.

mcqs.stem: During electrolysis, where do the positively charged ions move to?

options.text: To the positive electrode, which attracts them
options.rationale: The words 'positive ion' are matched to 'positive electrode' instead of using opposite charges attract.

options.text: To the anode, which is the negative electrode
options.rationale: The names anode and cathode are attached to the wrong signs.

options.text: To the anode, where they give up electrons
options.rationale: Both the electrode name and the electron transfer are the wrong way round for a positive ion.

options.text: To the cathode, the negative electrode
options.rationale: Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative electrode, which is called the cathode.

mcqs.stem: Ions are discharged at the electrodes during electrolysis. What is produced?

options.text: New compounds that build up on each electrode
options.rationale: Most reactions met in class make compounds, so a compound is expected here too.

options.text: Elements, as the ions lose their charge
options.rationale: Discharge removes the charge from an ion, leaving neutral atoms that make up an element.

options.text: The original compound, moved to the electrodes
options.rationale: Electrolysis is read as transport of the compound rather than a chemical change.

options.text: Electrons, which flow back out into the wire
options.rationale: The electron picture from the external circuit is used for the products of the cell.

mcqs.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?

options.text: Bromine, because the non-metals form there
options.rationale: The rule is reversed, putting the non-metal at the negative electrode.

options.text: Lead, the metal, collects at the cathode
options.rationale: Lead ions are positive, so they move to the negative electrode and are discharged as lead metal.

options.text: Hydrogen, made from water in this melt
options.rationale: The aqueous rules are applied to a molten compound that contains no water at all.

options.text: Lead ions, Pb²⁺, coating the whole electrode
options.rationale: The ion attracted to the electrode is named as the product, missing the discharge step.

mcqs.stem: What is seen at the anode when molten lead bromide is electrolysed?

options.text: A silvery bead of molten lead collects on it
options.rationale: The metal is placed at the positive electrode, ignoring the charge on its ion.

options.text: Colourless oxygen gas bubbles away from it
options.rationale: Oxygen from water is expected, although the molten compound contains no water.

options.text: Bromide ions are given off as a brown gas
options.rationale: The ion is named as the product rather than the element formed when it is discharged.

options.text: Orange-brown bromine vapour is given off
options.rationale: Bromide ions are negative, move to the anode and are discharged there as bromine.

mcqs.stem: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolysed. Which products are formed?

options.text: Magnesium at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive
options.rationale: The metal ion is positive so magnesium forms at the cathode; chloride ions are negative so chlorine forms at the anode.

options.text: Chlorine at the negative electrode, magnesium at the positive
options.rationale: The products are swapped, putting the metal at the positive electrode.

options.text: Hydrogen at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive
options.rationale: The rule for solutions is used even though there is no water in the melt.

options.text: Magnesium at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive
options.rationale: Oxygen is expected at the anode out of habit, although no oxygen is present.

mcqs.stem: Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed. Which products are formed?

options.text: Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: The products of electrolysing water are given for a compound that contains no water.

options.text: Oxygen at the cathode with aluminium at the anode
options.rationale: The metal and the non-metal are placed at the wrong electrodes.

options.text: Aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: Aluminium ions are positive and are discharged at the cathode; oxide ions are negative and give oxygen at the anode.

options.text: Aluminium at the cathode, nothing at the anode
options.rationale: The oxide ion is thought to stay in the melt rather than be discharged.

mcqs.stem: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?

options.text: Electrolysis is the cheaper of the two methods
options.rationale: Industry is assumed always to use the cheapest route, so the method used must be the cheap one.

options.text: Carbon needs a higher temperature than the furnace reaches
options.rationale: Assumes carbon could reduce aluminium if only hot enough, so blames temperature (m11).

options.text: Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon
options.rationale: Carbon only removes oxygen from the oxides of metals less reactive than carbon; aluminium is above it.

options.text: Carbon would leave the metal much too impure to use
options.rationale: Purity is offered as the reason, so reduction is still thought possible in principle.

mcqs.stem: Why does extracting a metal by electrolysis use so much energy?

options.text: The ore must first be purified using costly chemicals
options.rationale: Purification is a separate stage; the specification points to melting and the current.

options.text: Energy is needed to melt the compound and produce the current
options.rationale: Large amounts of energy are used both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.

options.text: Electrolysis needs far more ore than reduction by carbon
options.rationale: The cost is put down to how much ore is used rather than to energy.

options.text: The molten metal must be kept hot while it is moved
options.rationale: Handling the hot metal is a real cost, but not the energy cost the specification names.

mcqs.stem: In the manufacture of aluminium, what is the electrolyte and what is the positive electrode made of?

options.text: Aluminium oxide dissolved in warm water, with a steel anode
options.rationale: Electrolysis met in class uses solutions, so a solution is assumed for the industrial cell.

options.text: Molten cryolite on its own, with an anode made of carbon
options.rationale: Cryolite is taken to be the source of the aluminium rather than a way of lowering the melting point.

options.text: Solid aluminium oxide packed around the carbon anode
options.rationale: The compound is not melted, so the ions could not move to the electrodes.

options.text: A molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, carbon anode
options.rationale: The specification states a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite with carbon as the positive electrode.

mcqs.stem: Why is cryolite mixed with the aluminium oxide?

options.text: It lowers the melting point, so less energy is needed
options.rationale: Aluminium oxide alone melts at a very high temperature; the mixture melts lower, saving energy.

options.text: It acts as a catalyst and speeds the process up
options.rationale: Anything added to make a process work better is filed under catalyst.

options.text: It supplies all the aluminium ions that are discharged
options.rationale: Cryolite is named alongside the aluminium and is taken to be the source of the metal.

options.text: It stops the hot aluminium reacting with the air
options.rationale: A sensible-sounding purpose, but the reason given by the specification is the melting point.

mcqs.stem: Why must the positive electrode in the aluminium cell be replaced continually?

options.text: Oxygen made there reacts with the carbon and wears it away
options.rationale: Oxygen is discharged at the anode and reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is eaten away.

options.text: The heat of the molten mixture slowly melts the carbon
options.rationale: Wearing away is explained by temperature rather than by a chemical reaction.

options.text: The carbon dissolves in the melt because it is positive
options.rationale: Reactive-electrode cells are half remembered and applied to an inert carbon anode.

options.text: Aluminium coats the carbon and stops it conducting
options.rationale: The metal is placed at the positive electrode, so it is imagined coating the anode.

mcqs.stem: When an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what decides which ions are discharged?

options.text: The size of the charge carried by each of the ions
options.rationale: Charge decides which electrode an ion moves to, not which ion is discharged there.

options.text: The mass of each of the ions present in the solution
options.rationale: Mass has no part in the rule; the specification refers to reactivity.

options.text: The metal is discharged whatever else is there
options.rationale: The molten-state rule is carried over to solutions.

options.text: The relative reactivity of the elements involved
options.rationale: The specification states that the ions discharged depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.

mcqs.stem: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

options.text: Hydrogen, because copper is less reactive than it
options.rationale: The reactivity comparison is reversed, so hydrogen is chosen for the wrong reason.

options.text: Copper, as it is less reactive than hydrogen
options.rationale: The less reactive element is discharged, and copper is below hydrogen in reactivity.

options.text: Chlorine, since chloride ions are drawn there
options.rationale: Negative ions are sent to the negative electrode, ignoring that opposite charges attract.

options.text: Oxygen, released as the water breaks apart
options.rationale: Water is thought to split straight into hydrogen and oxygen gases at either electrode.

mcqs.stem: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

options.text: Sodium, because it is the metal in the compound used
options.rationale: The metal is expected at the cathode whatever its reactivity.

options.text: Sulfur, which forms from the sulfate ions in solution
options.rationale: The compound name is split in two and both halves are expected as products.

options.text: Hydrogen, as sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
options.rationale: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions from the water are discharged instead.

options.text: Oxygen, which the water always gives off there
options.rationale: Water is treated as splitting into both gases at once, wherever the electrode.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?

options.text: Sodium, which is drawn to the positive electrode
options.rationale: The positive ion is sent to the positive electrode.

options.text: Hydrogen, coming from the water in the solution
options.rationale: The gas from water is remembered but assigned to the wrong electrode.

options.text: Oxygen, which always forms at that electrode
options.rationale: The halide exception is dropped and oxygen is given for every solution.

options.text: Chlorine, as the solution holds halide ions
options.rationale: Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.

mcqs.stem: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?

options.text: Oxygen, as no halide ions are present
options.rationale: Sulfate is not a halide, so hydroxide ions from the water are discharged and oxygen is produced.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide, made from the sulfate ions
options.rationale: The sulfate ion is expected to be discharged like a halide.

options.text: Copper, plating onto the positive electrode
options.rationale: The positive metal ion is sent to the positive electrode.

options.text: Hydrogen, from the breakdown of the water
options.rationale: Water is credited with giving hydrogen at whichever electrode is being asked about.

mcqs.stem: In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions come from?

options.text: From the dissolved compound splitting into its ions
options.rationale: Only the compound added is tracked, so water is not seen as a source of ions.

options.text: From water molecules that break down in the solution
options.rationale: In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.

options.text: From hydrogen and oxygen gas dissolved in water
options.rationale: The gases are thought to be there already and simply released.

options.text: From the electrodes, which release them into the liquid
options.rationale: The electrode is treated as a source of particles rather than an inert surface where electrons are transferred.

mcqs.stem: A student plans Required practical 3 and writes an idea down before starting. Which statement is a hypothesis the investigation could test?

options.text: Copper chloride solution is a clear blue liquid
options.rationale: This is an observation recorded during the work, not a testable idea set out beforehand.

options.text: Bubbles appeared at the negative electrode
options.rationale: An observation of what was seen, mistaken for a testable hypothesis (m32).

options.text: Solutions of halides will give a halogen at the anode
options.rationale: It is a testable prediction, made in advance, that the results of the practical can support or disprove.

options.text: Which gas is given off at the negative electrode?
options.rationale: This is the question the investigation asks; the hypothesis is the answer proposed in advance.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 3, the gas collected at the cathode gave a squeaky pop with a lit splint. What does this show?

options.text: Hydrogen formed, so the metal is more reactive
options.rationale: A squeaky pop identifies hydrogen, which is discharged when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.

options.text: Oxygen formed, because oxygen relights the splint
options.rationale: The two splint tests are swapped, and oxygen is expected at the cathode.

options.text: Chlorine formed, since it bleaches damp litmus paper
options.rationale: A different gas test is recalled, and a halogen is placed at the negative electrode.

options.text: The metal itself formed and burned with the lit splint
options.rationale: The metal is expected at the cathode whatever its reactivity.

mcqs.stem: At the cathode, positively charged ions gain electrons. How is this reaction described?

options.text: Oxidation, because the electrons are gained
options.rationale: The two terms are swapped, since reduction sounds like something being taken away.

options.text: Reduction, because electrons are gained
options.rationale: Reduction is gain of electrons, so reactions at the cathode are reductions.

options.text: Oxidation, as the cathode is negative
options.rationale: The sign of the electrode is used in place of the electron transfer.

options.text: Neutralisation, as the charge has gone
options.rationale: Loss of charge is labelled with the only term the student has for charges cancelling out.

mcqs.stem: At the anode, negatively charged ions lose electrons. How is this reaction described?

options.text: Reduction, because electrons are lost
options.rationale: Loss of electrons is labelled reduction, swapping the two terms.

options.text: Reduction, since the anode is positive
options.rationale: The sign of the electrode is used instead of the electron transfer.

options.text: Oxidation, as electrons are lost by the ions
options.rationale: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so reactions at the anode are oxidations.

options.text: Oxidation, because oxygen is always made here
options.rationale: Oxidation is defined by oxygen alone, and oxygen is assumed to be the product every time.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of half equations represents the reactions at the two electrodes correctly?

options.text: 2H⁺ → H₂ + 2e⁻ at the cathode and 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O at the anode
options.rationale: The electrons are on the wrong side of both equations, so the cathode appears to lose them.

options.text: H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode and OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻ at the anode
options.rationale: Neither equation balances for atoms, because only the charges have been matched.

options.text: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the cathode, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the anode
options.rationale: The two correct equations are attached to the wrong electrodes.

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode, and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the anode
options.rationale: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode and negative ions lose electrons at the anode; both equations balance.

mcqs.stem: Which half equation shows hydrogen being produced at the cathode?

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: Two hydrogen ions gain two electrons to form one molecule of hydrogen; atoms and charge both balance.
The charges balance but the hydrogen atoms do not: two H⁺ cannot give two molecules.

options.text: 2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: The atoms balance but the charge does not, as only one electron is supplied for two positive charges.

options.text: H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: Neither the atoms nor the molecule are right, although the charges cancel.

mcqs.stem: Which half equation shows hydroxide ions being discharged at the anode?

options.text: 4OH⁻ → 2O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
options.rationale: There are only four oxygen atoms available, so two molecules of oxygen cannot be formed.

options.text: 2OH⁻ + 2e⁻ → O₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: The electrons have been placed on the left, which would make the anode gain them.

options.text: OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻
options.rationale: The charge cancels but the atoms are badly unbalanced.

options.text: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
options.rationale: Four hydroxide ions lose four electrons, giving one molecule of oxygen and two of water; atoms and charge balance.

mcqs.stem: The anode reaction may be written as 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ or as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O. How are the two related?

options.text: The second one supplies electrons instead of removing them
options.rationale: The minus sign is read as electrons being added on the left.

options.text: The first is the anode one, the second the cathode one
options.rationale: The two forms are taken to belong to different electrodes.

options.text: They are the same reaction, written in two ways
options.rationale: Losing four electrons can be shown by subtracting them on the left or adding them on the right.

options.text: The second one applies to a molten compound only
options.rationale: The difference is put down to the state of the electrolyte rather than to notation.

mcqs.stem: Complete and balance the half equation for the reaction at the cathode in the aluminium cell.

options.text: 3Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al
options.rationale: Three ions carry nine positive charges, so three electrons cannot discharge them.

options.text: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
options.rationale: Each aluminium ion carries three positive charges, so it gains three electrons to form an aluminium atom.

options.text: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al
options.rationale: The charge is right but the atoms are not: one ion gives one atom.

options.text: Al³⁺ + e⁻ → Al
options.rationale: Only one electron is supplied, so the charge does not balance.

mcqs.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode?

options.text: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
options.rationale: Each lead ion carries two positive charges, so it gains two electrons at the cathode to form a lead atom.

options.text: Pb²⁺ + e⁻ → Pb
options.rationale: The atoms balance, but one electron cannot cancel two positive charges, so the charge does not balance.

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: This is the correct anode equation. Naming the cathode as the positive electrode puts the bromide reaction there.

options.text: 2Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Pb
options.rationale: One electron has been counted for each ion. The charge on the ion sets the number, so two ions need four electrons.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode?

options.text: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Two chloride ions each lose one electron at the anode, giving one molecule of chlorine; atoms and charge balance.

options.text: 2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
options.rationale: The electrons are on the left, which would mean the chloride ions gained them. At the anode they are lost.

options.text: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 4e⁻
options.rationale: The atoms balance but the charge does not: two chloride ions can release only two electrons between them.

options.text: 2Na⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Na
options.rationale: Sodium ions are positive, so they travel to the cathode, not to the anode this equation is asking about.
